applied.before: The surah opens by declaring that what people have before them is “the verses of the Book and a clear Qur’an”. Revelation is clear in itself; the problem is not its inability to explain, but the barriers erected around it that prevent it from reaching people or turn their hearts away. Preservation is one of the surah’s prominent themes: preserving the Reminder, guarding heaven against the devils’ eavesdropping, protecting Allah’s sincere servants from Iblis’s authority, saving whomever Allah wills from punishment, and protecting the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) against the mockers. This need not be the surah’s only subject, but it is a clear thread recurring in several places. It helps us understand the struggle between revelation that reaches people, devils that seek to turn them away from it, and human beings who choose either to respond or to turn away.
applied.after: The surah opens by declaring that what people have before them is “the verses of the Book and a clear Qur’an”. Revelation is clear in itself; the problem is not its inability to explain, but the barriers erected around it that prevent it from reaching people or turn their hearts away. Preservation is one of the surah’s prominent themes: preserving the Reminder, guarding heaven against the devils’ eavesdropping, protecting Allah’s sincere servants from Iblis’s authority, saving whomever Allah wills from punishment, and protecting the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) against the mockers. This theme recurs throughout the surah. It helps us understand the struggle between revelation that reaches people, devils that seek to turn them away from it, and human beings who choose either to respond or to turn away.

applied.before: The verse “They will not believe in it, although the examples of the earlier people are well established” connects their condition with an earlier pattern: the presence of signs does not compel a heart that has chosen wrongdoing to believe. A believer should therefore not imagine that the problem is always a shortage of evidence or a failure to present it effectively. The explanation may be clear, yet denial remain. This does not remove the duty to convey the message clearly, but it prevents us from making guidance depend on the number of proofs alone.
applied.after: The verse “They will not believe in it, although the examples of the earlier people are well established” connects their condition with an earlier pattern: the presence of signs does not compel a heart that has chosen wrongdoing to believe. The message must be conveyed clearly. A shortage of evidence or an unclear presentation does not explain every refusal. A person may understand the evidence and still reject it, so guidance cannot be measured by the number of proofs alone.

applied.before: The verse “Even if We were to open for them a gateway to the heaven, through which they kept ascending” takes the example to the furthest reaches of sensory demands: an open gateway in heaven and an ascent they witness for themselves. Even this would not guarantee their acceptance. Someone demanding a sign out of obstinacy can, after seeing it, search for another label for what they have seen instead of reconsidering their position. The point is not to diminish the value of tangible signs, but to expose how a stubborn heart can turn even direct observation into fresh material for rejection.
applied.after: The verse “Even if We were to open for them a gateway to the heaven, through which they kept ascending” takes the example to the furthest reaches of sensory demands: an open gateway in heaven and an ascent they witness for themselves. Even a sign as powerful as this would not guarantee their acceptance. Someone demanding a sign out of obstinacy can, after seeing it, search for another label for what they have seen instead of reconsidering their position. Such a person can turn even direct observation into another reason for rejection.

applied.before: The verse “We have placed constellations in the heaven and adorned it for the onlookers” presents another kind of adornment. Allah has adorned heaven so that people look upwards and their hearts rise towards the signs of His dominion. In contrast, Iblis later says: “I will surely make [sins] alluring to them on earth”. The very direction of one’s gaze thus becomes part of the struggle: adornment that leads to remembrance, and adornment used to immerse the heart in earthly concerns. The point is not to abandon worldly life, but to prevent its attractions from monopolising the gaze and turning it away from revelation and what lies above.
applied.after: The verse “We have placed constellations in the heaven and adorned it for the onlookers” presents another kind of adornment. Allah has adorned heaven so that people look upwards and their hearts rise towards the signs of His dominion. In contrast, Iblis later says: “I will surely make [sins] alluring to them on earth”. The very direction of one’s gaze thus becomes part of the struggle: adornment that leads to remembrance, and adornment used to immerse the heart in earthly concerns. While benefiting from worldly life, a person can keep their eyes open to revelation and to the signs in the heavens, so that earthly attractions do not claim their whole attention.

applied.before: The verse “Surely the people of Al-Hijr also rejected the messengers” evokes the idea of an enclosure. [The Arabic word ḥijr is associated here with something firmly closed off.] The people of Al-Hijr built in the mountains what they believed would be fortresses and safety, yet this did not protect them against Allah’s command. Elsewhere, the surah repeatedly depicts barriers erected to prevent revelation from reaching people. An enclosure may be physical, something behind which a person shelters from punishment, while intellectual and social barriers may surround the call to faith. In neither case does merely building a barrier provide true security.
applied.after: The verse “Surely the people of Al-Hijr also rejected the messengers” brings to mind the meaning of the name Al-Hijr, a firmly enclosed place. The people of Al-Hijr built in the mountains what they believed would be fortresses and safety, yet this did not protect them against Allah’s command. Throughout the surah, intellectual and social barriers are raised to keep revelation from reaching people. The physical fortress was meant to shield its builders from punishment. These other barriers shut out the revelation warning them of it. In neither case does merely building a barrier provide true security.

applied.before: The verse “Nothing of what they earned was of any avail to them” sums up the end of every protection imagined to be independent of Allah. What they gathered, built, and earned did not repel the command when it came. The verse does not call for abandoning work or practical means, but for abandoning the illusion that possessing a means is the same as being saved. What one holds remains limited in value. When the known appointed time comes, no earnings can delay it.
applied.after: The verse “Nothing of what they earned was of any avail to them” sums up the end of every protection imagined to be independent of Allah. What they gathered, built, and earned did not repel the command when it came. Earning a living and taking practical steps have their proper place, while the means themselves cannot guarantee deliverance. What one holds remains limited in value. When the known appointed time comes, no earnings can delay it.

applied.before: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) related that after Allah fashioned Adam, Iblis began circling him. Seeing that he was hollow, Iblis recognised that Adam was a creature unable to keep himself fully under control [Muslim: 2611]. Human beings have an inner space and needs. The problem is not that they need something, but what they fill that need with. Just as the body is filled with food, the heart needs provision. If revelation does not fill it, it will keep looking longingly for an endless succession of attractions to make up the lack. An unconfirmed report about the occasion of this verse’s revelation says that the Muslims looked at caravans carrying wealth and goods, which were then contrasted with the Quran they possessed. A caravan passes away, whereas revelation forms people, its effects are renewed, and its riches do not run out.

applied.before: Before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is told “Do not look longingly”, Allah reminds him of His gift: “the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur’an”. The seven oft-repeated verses have been understood as Al-Fatihah, alongside other interpretations. The point here is that the revelation he received is richer and more lasting than enjoyment that passes away. A Hadith states: “Whoever does not recite Qur'an in a nice voice is not from us” [al-Bukhari: 7527]. [One interpretation of the Arabic verb yataghannā is to find sufficiency in the Quran rather than in other things.] This meaning connects with an inward human need.
